text: Mukul Chandra Dey (23 July 1895 – 1 March 1989) was one of five children of Purnashashi Devi and Kula Chandra Dey. He studied at Rabindranath Tagore's Santiniketan and is recognized as a pioneer of drypoint-etching in India. The entire Dey family exhibited artistic talent, with his brother Manishi Dey becoming a well-known painter and his sisters, Annapura and Rani Chanda, excelling in arts and crafts. Mukul Dey married Bina Roy from Khanakul, Bengal; they had one daughter, Manjari, affectionately named Bukuma, who later married Shantanu Ukil, a leading painter of the Bengal School of Art. He was the first Indian artist to travel abroad specifically to study printmaking. In 1916, while in Japan, he studied under Yokoyama Taikan and Kanzan Shimomura in Tokyo and Yokohama, and during his stay at Tomitaro Hara’s Sankeien, he lived with Rabindranath Tagore and studied classical Chinese and Nihonga style Japanese paintings, particularly the works of Sesshu Toyo. After returning to India, Dey trained in etching in Chicago under James Blanding Sloan and Bertha Jaques, introduced by American artists Roi Partridge and Imogen Cunningham, and remained a life-member of the Chicago Society of Etchers. In 1920, he traveled again to study etching and engraving under Frank Short and Muirhead Bone at the Slade School of Fine Art and the Royal College of Art in London, where he studied under Professor Henry Tonks. An exhibition of his drawings and paintings, including ten copies of Ajanta and one of Bagh Caves paintings, was held at 59 Onslow Square, London, on 4 February 1924, with the assistance of Lady Grant; his work had previously been displayed at the Royal Academy and the New English Art Club. According to Polish sculptor Stanislaw Szukalski, when Mukul was in America, he showed him his drawings, which impressed Szukalski, who then advised him against going to Paris to "finish his study," warning that such a move would lead to blind admiration for movements like Kandinski and Picasso, and urged Mukul to develop self-confidence to view European art with contempt and select only worthy examples. This advice convinced Mukul to return to Santiniketan, to Tagore’s delight. Dey used a Western medium—drypoint etching—to portray Indian life, unlike Haren Das, whose woodcut technique was more indigenous. His subjects included river scenes in Bengal, traditional baul singers, Calcutta markets, and the lives of Santhal villagers in Birbhum near Santiniketan. He was an active member of the Vichitra Club at Jorasanko, where young artists like Nandalal Bose, Asit Kumar Haldar, and Narayan Kashinath Deval were encouraged to experiment with new art forms. In 1925, Dey published a book on the Ajanta and Bagh cave paintings, which inspired him deeply, and later illustrated and published several other books. In 1928, he was appointed the first Indian Principal of the Government School of Art, Calcutta, where he removed teachers closely associated with Company School painting and established a women's section, previously open only to men. Gracefully drawn images of Bengali villagers in dry-point have become his most recognized works, with some pieces hand-coloured using watercolors, coloured pencils, or thin ink washes. He is also remembered for portraits of prominent Indian figures, including members of the Tagore and Tata families, Albert Einstein, Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, and Josephine MacLeod, the promoter of Swami Vivekananda’s Ramakrishna order at Belur Math—MacLeod having first brought Okakura Kakuzo to India in 1901–1902. Manishi Dey, Mukul’s younger brother, was a member of the Progressive Artists' Group and a prominent painter of the Bengal School of Art, traveling extensively throughout India in contrast to his more steady brother. Dey’s works are held in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, the Indian Museum, Kolkata, the National Gallery of Modern Art in Mumbai, and the National Gallery of Art in New Delhi. The Mukul Dey Archives are preserved at Chitralekha, his former home in Santiniketan. He also served as an illustrator for several book projects, including the scholarly work *Shantiniketan Bolpur School of Rabindranath Tagore*, which he illustrated for the later Nobel Prize winner in 1916.
